props.title: The Fourth Man

sections.content: Paul Verhoeven's The Fourth Man (1983) stands as a masterful psychological thriller that prefigures his later Hollywood works like Basic Instinct (1992). This Dutch gem follows a bisexual writer's descent into paranoid obsession, blending Catholic imagery with erotic horror in ways that would become Verhoeven's signature. The film's hallucinatory style and sexual frankness shocked audiences, while establishing themes that influenced later European psychological thrillers like Possession (1981) and The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover (1989).

sections.content: Verhoeven's masterful direction creates an atmosphere of mounting dread through religious symbolism and erotic imagery. The film's exploration of sexuality and death bears striking similarities to Dressed to Kill (1980) and Cat People (1982), though Verhoeven's approach is distinctly European in its unflinching portrayal of both psychological and physical violence. Renée Soutendijk's performance as the mysterious Christine Halsslag set a template for the dangerous feminine mystique that would later define Sharon Stone's career-making role in Basic Instinct (1992).

The film's complex layering of reality, fantasy, and religious visions creates a destabilizing effect that influenced later psychological thrillers like Mulholland Drive (2001) and Black Swan (2010). Verhoeven's ability to blur the lines between protagonist Gerard Reve's alcoholic delusions and genuine supernatural threats creates a compelling uncertainty that keeps viewers questioning until the final frame. sections.content: The Fourth Man's provocative blend of Catholic imagery with explicit sexuality establishes themes that would later appear in films like The Devils (1971) and Bad Lieutenant (1992). Verhoeven's background in Dutch Protestantism informs his subversive approach to religious iconography, creating a film that's both reverent and blasphemous. The director's unflinching examination of sexuality and faith would later influence works like Benedetta (2021) and Saint Maud (2019).
